title: Dietary advice and nutrition therapy: getting useful, individual support
intro: Nutrition advice can help people build everyday eating habits, while nutrition therapy addresses the needs created by a medical condition. The useful starting point is your health, circumstances and goals, rather than a universal meal plan. Good support should be understandable, affordable where possible and adapted to the foods and routines that matter to you.

sections.heading: Choose support for the problem you actually have
paragraphs: General advice may cover meal planning, food variety and practical changes during different stages of life. Medical nutrition care may help with diabetes, kidney disease, coeliac disease, allergies, digestive symptoms, cancer or poor intake. These conditions can have different, sometimes conflicting needs. Advice to reduce energy intake is not appropriate for everyone: someone losing weight unintentionally may need more nourishment. Children, pregnancy, swallowing difficulties and eating disorders require relevant expertise. Food can support treatment, but a diet programme should not promise to cure every illness or replace prescribed medicines without clinical review.

sections.heading: Check the provider and the practical arrangements
paragraphs: Ask about recognised training, professional registration where applicable, experience with your condition and communication with your medical team. Titles and regulation differ between countries; a convincing website alone does not establish competence. Ask who will deliver the sessions, whether an interpreter or accessible format is available, and whether someone you choose can attend. Before paying, confirm referral requirements, total costs, follow-up and any insurer or public-service coverage directly with the relevant service. The source article describes German arrangements, which should not be assumed to apply elsewhere. Disclose or ask about product sales and financial interests, especially if buying supplements is made a condition of care.

sections.heading: Prepare a realistic picture of daily life
paragraphs: Bring diagnoses, recent relevant results, medicines, supplements, allergies and weight changes if known. A brief food and symptom record can help, but perfect tracking is unnecessary and may be unsuitable if it worsens an eating disorder. Explain working hours, budget, cooking and storage facilities, cultural or religious practices, food preferences, dental problems and who shops or prepares meals. Mention nausea, diarrhoea, difficulty chewing or swallowing and trouble obtaining enough food. The goal is to understand barriers, not judge willpower. Do not remove gluten before coeliac testing without medical advice, because this can make the tests inaccurate; do not reintroduce a known dangerous allergen on your own.

sections.heading: Agree on a plan that can be reviewed
paragraphs: Choose a manageable goal and discuss how it fits your treatment. Examples include regular meals around shifts, replacing an affordable staple, fortifying food for poor intake or finding safe substitutes for a confirmed allergy. Ask which changes are essential, which are optional, and how to preserve protein, energy and micronutrients when foods are excluded. Diabetes medicines may need adjustment when intake changes; arrange this with the prescriber. Special diets for kidney disease or fluid restrictions need individual advice rather than a generic internet list. Agree what improvement to monitor, when to return and what to do if symptoms or intake worsen. Plans should be revised when they are impractical.

sections.heading: Recognise when routine advice is not enough
paragraphs: Unintentional weight loss, prolonged poor appetite, recurrent vomiting, dehydration, blood in stools or worsening swallowing difficulty need medical assessment rather than only a meal plan. Malnutrition can occur at any body size. After prolonged very low intake, restarting nutrition may require supervised care because dangerous shifts in body salts can occur; do not attempt an aggressive catch-up regimen yourself. Choking, serious breathing difficulty, collapse or a severe allergic reaction require emergency care. Nutrition supplements or tube feeding are sometimes part of clinical treatment, with monitoring and a clear purpose. Ask for coordinated medical and dietetic help if several conditions or medicines make eating complicated.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: a plan that fits the budget
examples.text: Arben works changing shifts and cannot afford a prescribed list of expensive foods. He and a dietitian plan a small number of familiar, affordable meals that fit his diabetes treatment and work breaks. They agree a review rather than treating difficulty following the first plan as failure.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: a different nutritional priority
examples.text: Elena has lost weight during illness and is struggling with meals. Instead of joining a weight-loss programme, she seeks medical assessment and dietetic support for adequate intake. The plan considers symptoms, practical help with food and whether clinical nutrition products are needed.

questions: What expertise do I need, and how can I verify the provider's qualifications?
How will this plan fit my illnesses, medicines, budget and usual foods?
What should we monitor, when will we review it and which symptoms need medical help?
